statements.answer: I am here because work suggested an assessment after the missed deadlines piled up. I want to know what is going on, and whether there is anything that actually helps.
statements.question: What brings you to this assessment now, and is there anything about your background you think is relevant?

statements.answer: I zone out in the middle of things more than I would like. Someone will be explaining something and I will realise I only caught half of it. It is embarrassing when they notice.
statements.question: Think about an ordinary day. What is it like for you to stay focused on one thing?

statements.answer: Organizing things is not my strong point. I have tried planners and apps and they work until I forget to open them, which takes about three days.
statements.question: How do you find organizing your time, your tasks, or your belongings?

statements.answer: At work I miss deadlines more than I would like to admit. Someone will ask where a report is and I will realise I never even started it, even though I meant to all week.
statements.question: What kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?

statements.answer: I forget stupid little things all the time — why I walked into a room, where I put my phone while I am holding it. It drives my partner mad.
statements.question: Do you ever forget appointments, obligations, or where you put things? What is that like?

statements.answer: In long meetings I fidget quite a lot, clicking pens and shifting about in my chair. An hour sat still feels endless to me.
statements.question: When you need to sit still or stay with one thing, what is that like for you?

statements.answer: I do jump in a bit. If I have the answer I will just say it rather than waiting. Sometimes that lands badly and I wish I had held back.
statements.question: How are you with waiting your turn, or holding back when you want to jump in?

statements.answer: School was never a problem. I got through it like everyone else, and I do not remember any big issues with teachers or grades back then.
statements.question: Thinking back to childhood and school, what do you remember about yourself as a child?

statements.answer: Over the years it has been up and down, I think. Some jobs it was worse, some stretches were okay. I could not map it out exactly, but it has definitely been there a long time.
statements.question: How have these kinds of experiences changed over the years, as far as you can tell?

statements.answer: It is worst at work, where there are deadlines and people watching. At home it matters less, though the flat is chaos. So it shows up differently depending on the pressure.
statements.question: Are these experiences different depending on where you are — for example at home versus work or study?

statements.answer: Actually, I repeated a year after missing so much coursework that they held me back. I had sort of forgotten about that until now. A whole year gone, because I just had not handed things in.
statements.question: Can you describe a recent time when these experiences affected your work or studies?

statements.answer: My partner says I do not listen, and they are probably right. I will nod along and then have no idea what was agreed. We argue about it more than I would like.
statements.question: How do these experiences affect the people around you, or your day-to-day life outside work?

statements.answer: Whether any of this goes back to childhood, I am not sure. I honestly cannot say if I was like this as a kid or if it started later.
statements.question: Are there things like sleep, stress, mood, or health that seem to make these experiences better or worse?

statements.answer: I try keeping lists, and they help for a day or two. Then I lose the list, or stop looking at it, and I am back where I started.
statements.question: What do you do to cope with or work around these experiences — routines, reminders, help from others?
